about: How `--name` tokens bind. Long names match exactly — there is no abbreviation inference — and a value may be attached with `=` or given as the following word.

vectors.doc: A flag with no argument binds true when present.
An absent boolean flag is not bound at all, rather than bound false.
`--flag=value` binds the text after the first `=`.
`--flag value` binds the following word.
Only the first `=` separates; the rest belongs to the value, so `--set=a=b` yields `a=b`.
`--flag=` binds the empty string. Present-but-empty is a different state from absent, and only the attached form can express it.
`--force=` on a flag that holds no value leaves nothing behind. An empty value means something only to a flag that takes one, and a stray empty word would otherwise be read as a positional.
An attached value binds even when it looks like a flag: `=` has already settled where the value came from.

reference.diverges: usage-lib binds `force` instead and leaves `jobs` unset, treating the attached value as a separate flag token.

vectors.doc: A flag needing a value that ends the command line is an error.
A detached value must not itself look like a flag, so a forgotten value is reported rather than swallowed. Use the attached form to pass a value that begins with a dash.
A negative number is a value, not a flag, so it may be given detached. Without this exception no CLI could accept `--offset -1`.

An unrecognized long flag is offered to the positionals like any other word. A spec is often parsing a command line whose flags belong to something else, so a token it has not heard of is more likely data in transit than a mistake.

A unique prefix of a long name is not accepted as the flag. Abbreviation inference makes adding a flag a breaking change for anyone who typed a prefix that was unique until now, so the grammar has none — the token becomes a word, and here there is no argument to hold it.
A `var` flag collects each occurrence in order.
A flag whose argument is variadic takes several values from one occurrence, which is what the trailing ellipsis in `<pattern>...` declares.

reference.diverges: usage-lib reports `unexpected_arg` for the second value. The spec reference documents this form, so the gap is in the parser rather than in the declaration.

vectors.doc: A `var` flag whose argument is not variadic takes exactly one value per occurrence. It is repetition, not greed, so the word after its value is still available to a positional.
A flag with `negate` binds false when the negating form is used.
With neither form given, a negatable flag takes its declared default.
A CLI that owns all of its flags declares `unknown_flags "error"` and gets typo detection: the token is refused rather than passed along as data.
Even when refusing unknown flags, a negative number is a value. This is the carve-out oclif had to add back after making rejection its default.
